meta.what: Display context for the Mars first pass; these extra figures do not change any score.
meta.order: Every column follows squares.ids, copied in order from mars.json squares.ids.
layout: Column-major data, little-endian, without a header or padding.
For row i, read type at offset + i * bytes_per_value.
The reserved unknown value means null and is never zero.
For numeric columns, divide the stored integer by scale.
For lookup columns, the stored integer indexes lookup; its JSON value is returned unchanged.
Lookup entries may be names, booleans, lists, or small records.
Field paths start with the input filename stem; dots describe nested object keys.
Numeric values retain the precision held in the inputs; the page controls their displayed precision.
monthly_peak_rule: Best month means the month with the highest known monthly value, not the safest UV exposure.
Ties keep calendar order; all months unknown gives an unknown month and value.
Month names come from mars.json squares.months.
meta.input_meta: The input_meta object copies every input meta block without changing any value.
meta.omitted: Monthly arrays and figures unused by the cards are omitted; their definitions remain in input_meta.

mars_environment.what: Mars part, environment side: UV, sunlight at the ground, clear-sky days and haze (aerosol optical depth). For every ranked half-degree square of data/derived/mars_cells.json (bare share at least 0.15). Each value is the NASA POWER monthly climatology of the 1 degree box, about 111 km tall, holding the square. It is not a measurement at the place; many squares share one box. It enters no score.
mars_environment.source: NASA POWER, POWER Climatology API v2.10.1, regional endpoint, community RE. Data set named in the answers: CERES SYN1deg (SYN1DEG; ALLSKY_KT and CLRSKY_DAYS: SYN1DEG and POWER).

parameter_list.how_the_names_were_settled: Names, definitions and units read from the service's own climatology parameter list (communities RE, AG and SB, all saved). Names and definitions searched for dust, aerosol, smoke, haze and particulate. Found AOD_55, AOD_55_ADJ and AOD_84 only, no dust-only parameter.

ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN.name_in_the_service: All Sky Surface Shortwave Downward Irradiance
ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN.definition_in_the_service: The total solar irradiance incident (direct plus diffuse) on a horizontal plane at the surface of the earth under all sky conditions. An alternative term for the total solar irradiance is the "Global Horizontal Irradiance" or GHI.
ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN.grid: 1 x 1 degree, centres at x.5 (read from the answers)
ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN.what_it_is_not: Not the sunlight on a tilted panel or in one hour, and not a measurement at the square. It is the energy reaching level ground in a mean day of the month, night included. Satellite-based, under the real mix of cloud and clear, for a 1 degree box about 111 km tall.

ALLSKY_SFC_UV_INDEX.grid: 1 x 1 degree, centres at x.5 (read from the answers)
ALLSKY_SFC_UV_INDEX.what_it_is_not: Not the noon UV index of a weather forecast. It is the mean over all 24 hours of the month's mean day, night included. Checked: the 24 hourly values of the service's hour-based set average to it within 2 percent in most box-months. So it is several times lower than the brightest hour, which uv_index_brightest_hour gives.

AOD_55.definition_in_the_service: The optical thickness at 0.55 um measured vertically; the component of the atmosphere to quantify the removal of radiant energy from an incident beam.
AOD_55.grid: 1 x 1 degree, centres at x.5 (read from the answers)
AOD_55.years_the_values_fit: 2001 to any end year from 2018 to 2021 (the check cannot tell them apart)
AOD_55.what_it_is_not: Not dust alone and not dust on the ground. It is the optical depth at 550 nm of all fine particles in the air column together. That is dust, smoke, sea salt, haze and pollution, as a monthly mean for a 1 degree box.

CLRSKY_DAYS.definition_in_the_service: The number of Clear Sky Days if the daytime cloud amount is less than 10 percent.
CLRSKY_DAYS.grid: 1 x 1 degree, centres at x.5 (read from the answers)
CLRSKY_DAYS.what_it_is_not: Not the days a camera at the square sees a clear sky. A day counts only when daytime cloud over the whole 1 degree box is under 10 percent. So a partly cloudy box, or a coastal box with sea cloud, counts as not clear. The service sums the count over all years; it is divided here by the years the check found.

CLRSKY_SFC_SW_DWN.name_in_the_service: Clear Sky Surface Shortwave Downward Irradiance
CLRSKY_SFC_SW_DWN.definition_in_the_service: The total solar irradiance incident (direct plus diffuse) on a horizontal plane at the surface of the earth under clear sky conditions. An alternative term for the total solar irradiance is the "Global Horizontal Irradiance" or GHI.
CLRSKY_SFC_SW_DWN.grid: 1 x 1 degree, centres at x.5 (read from the answers)
CLRSKY_SFC_SW_DWN.what_it_is_not: This is not what reaches the ground on a typical day. It is what would reach a level surface on the same days if there were no cloud.

ALLSKY_KT.definition_in_the_service: A fraction representing clearness of the atmosphere; the all sky insolation that is transmitted through the atmosphere to strike the surface of the earth divided by the average of top of the atmosphere total solar irradiance incident.
ALLSKY_KT.grid: 1 x 1 degree, centres at x.5 (read from the answers)
ALLSKY_KT.what_it_is_not: Not a share of clear days. It is the share of top-of-atmosphere sunlight that reaches level ground in a mean day, cloud, haze and air together.

ALLSKY_SFC_UVA.definition_in_the_service: The ultraviolet A (UVA 315nm-400nm) irradiance under all sky conditions.
ALLSKY_SFC_UVA.grid: 1 x 1 degree, centres at x.5 (read from the answers)
ALLSKY_SFC_UVA.what_it_is_not: Not weighted for harm to skin or life: the plain energy of UVA light (315-400 nm) a day.

ALLSKY_SFC_UVB.definition_in_the_service: The ultraviolet B (UVB 280nm-315nm) irradiance under all sky conditions.
ALLSKY_SFC_UVB.grid: 1 x 1 degree, centres at x.5 (read from the answers)
ALLSKY_SFC_UVB.what_it_is_not: Not weighted for harm to skin or life: the plain energy of UVB light (280-315 nm) a day.

AOD_55_ADJ.definition_in_the_service: The adjusted optical thickness at 0.55 um measured vertically; the component of the atmosphere to quantify the removal of radiant energy from an incident beam.
AOD_55_ADJ.grid: 1 x 1 degree, centres at x.5 (read from the answers)
AOD_55_ADJ.what_it_is_not: Not explained by the service beyond the word 'adjusted'. Kept beside AOD_55 for comparison only, and not used in any sentence. The Moon-part file uses AOD_55_ADJ instead.

TOA_SW_DWN.definition_in_the_service: The total solar irradiance incident (direct plus diffuse) on a horizontal plane at the top of the atmosphere (extraterrestrial radiation).
TOA_SW_DWN.grid: 1 x 1 degree, centres at x.5 (read from the answers)
TOA_SW_DWN.what_it_is_not: This is not sunlight at the ground. It is what a level surface would get above the atmosphere. We keep it to compare the ground figures with it.

ALLSKY_SFC_UV_INDEX_HR.name_in_the_service: All Sky Surface UV Index (Hour-Based Parameter Set)
ALLSKY_SFC_UV_INDEX_HR.grid: 1 x 1 degree, centres at x.5 (read from the answers)
ALLSKY_SFC_UV_INDEX_HR.what_it_is_not: Not one day's noon value and not the clearest day's. It is the highest of the 24 hourly values of the month's mean day, all sky, for a 1 degree box. Hours are local solar time, as the service labels them. The service gives no definition of the hour-based set beyond its name.

fields.sun_kwh_m2_day: ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN by month, kWh per m2 per day on level ground, all sky (January first)
fields.sun_kwh_m2_day_year: ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, the service's annual value, kWh per m2 per day
fields.uv_index: ALLSKY_SFC_UV_INDEX by month: UV index averaged over all 24 hours of the day, night included
fields.uv_index_year: ALLSKY_SFC_UV_INDEX, the service's annual value (24-hour mean)
fields.uv_index_brightest_hour: By month, the highest of the 24 hourly values of the month's mean day, local solar time. From the service's hour-based set ALLSKY_SFC_UV_INDEX_HR. It is the figure closest to a forecast's noon UV index.
fields.clear_days: CLRSKY_DAYS by month divided by the years the count was summed over. Days a month with daytime cloud over the 1 degree box under 10 percent. Null if those years are not settled.
fields.clear_days_year: The service's annual CLRSKY_DAYS divided by the same years: such days a year. The service gives its fill value for the year whenever the total passes 1800. There the sum of its 12 months is used (counts.squares_with_clear_days_year_from_month_sum).
fields.aod_550: AOD_55 by month: aerosol optical depth at 550 nm, all particles in the air column, dimensionless
fields.sun_clear_sky_kwh_m2_day_year: CLRSKY_SFC_SW_DWN annual: sunlight on level ground were there no cloud, kWh/m2/day
fields.clearness_index_year: ALLSKY_KT annual: share of top-of-atmosphere sunlight that reaches the ground
fields.aod_550_adjusted_year: AOD_55_ADJ annual ('adjusted', not explained by the service)
fields.top_of_atmosphere_kwh_m2_day_year: TOA_SW_DWN annual: sunlight on a level surface above the atmosphere, kWh/m2/day
fields.grid: [lat, lon] of the centre of the 1 degree box that holds the square centre (all values are that box's)

years_check.what: The climatology of each checked parameter against the service's monthly series 2001-2025 of the same box. Five named places, one request a place, saved in data/raw/power_global_environment/checks. For each last year: how many calendar months the series mean over 2001 to that year equals the climatology. For CLRSKY_DAYS the sum is compared, not the mean.

AOD_55.years_the_values_fit: 2001 to any end year from 2018 to 2021 (the check cannot tell them apart)

years_check.note: The service's answers name January 2001 to December 2025. data/derived/temperature_cells.json found its temperature values fit 2001 to 2020. Read years_the_values_fit as what the numbers show, and the named period as what the service says.

mars_environment.clear_days_rule: The service's CLRSKY_DAYS climatology is a count summed over all years of its period. Monthly values above 31 occur, such as 137 in January at 28.5 S 70.5 W. clear_days = that count / 20 years.
mars_environment.uv_rule: The UV index (uv_index) is ALLSKY_SFC_UV_INDEX of the service. It is a mean over all 24 hours of the day, and it includes the night. The UV index of the brightest hour (uv_index_brightest_hour) is the highest hourly value of ALLSKY_SFC_UV_INDEX_HR for the mean day of each month.
mars_environment.cell_to_grid: the 1 degree box that holds the square centre (twinfinder.cloud.grid_box); no square sits on a box edge
mars_environment.null_rule: unknown is null, never 0: a parameter or block not fetched, a fill value (-999), or clear days whose years are not settled
mars_environment.request_rules_followed: One parameter and one 10 x 10 degree block a request, one at a time with a 0.5 s pause. User-Agent twinfinder/0.1, no key, no login; wait and try again after a dropped network or 429. On 15 November 2026 UTC the five monthly checks and two probes ran beside the main fetch. So for a few seconds two requests were open at once; the service allows five.

sunlight_top_of_atmosphere.what: sunlight at the top of the atmosphere
sunlight_top_of_atmosphere.source: NASA NSSDCA Mars Fact Sheet and Earth Fact Sheet (saved: data/raw/mars_climate/factsheets/)
sunlight_top_of_atmosphere.mars_range_how: 586.2 W/m2 times (227.956 / distance)^2 at aphelion 249.261 and perihelion 206.650 million km

dust_optical_depth.source: Mars: Martinez et al. 2017, Space Science Reviews, section 3.1 (saved: data/raw/mars_sites/martinez2017_ssr_review.pdf)
dust_optical_depth.note: Mars: optical depth generally below 1 in the aphelion season (Ls 0-180) and above 3 at the peak of global dust storms (in-situ record of 7 landers); dust is in the sky all year. Earth: global mean optical depth at 550 nm about 0.1-0.2 (Earth figure from memory, not checked)

uv_cut_off.unit: nm, shortest wavelength of sunlight reaching the ground
uv_cut_off.source: literature, not checked against a saved file in this run: Cockell et al. 2000, Icarus 146, 343-359 (Mars); the ozone cut-off near 290 nm (Earth)
uv_cut_off.note: Mars has almost no ozone, so UV-C (200-280 nm), which never reaches Earth's ground, reaches the Mars surface; only CO2 stops light shorter than about 190-200 nm

sunlight_at_the_ground.what: daily sunlight on level ground at a Mars site (kWh/m2 a day or W/m2)

uv_index.what: a UV index or UV irradiance at the ground of a Mars site

cloud_free_days.what: a count of cloud-free (or dust-free) days at a Mars site

dust_only_optical_depth_earth.what: a dust-only optical depth for Earth (the service offers none)

sentences.sunlight: Earth's sunniest ranked box (-23.5, -67.5, Altiplano and Puna) gets 7.37 kWh per m2 a day on level ground. It keeps 0.8 of the sunlight arriving above its air. Above its air Mars gets 586.2 W/m2, 0.431 of Earth's 1361.0. How much reaches the Mars ground is not in our data.
sentences.uv: Earth's highest UV index is 19.7 in the brightest hour of the mean day (-23.5, -67.5, Altiplano and Puna). As a 24-hour mean it is 3.38. No Earth place matches Mars in kind: sunlight down to 190 nm reaches the Mars ground, 290 nm on Earth. Source: literature, not checked against a saved file in this run: Cockell et al. 2000, Icarus 146, 343-359 (Mars); the ozone cut-off near 290 nm (Earth). A Mars UV index is not in our data.
sentences.clear_days: Earth's clearest ranked box (23.5, 27.5, Sahara) has 276 days a year with daytime cloud under 10 percent over the whole box. A count of clear days on Mars is not in our data. Our files say dust is in the Mars sky all year (Mars: Martinez et al. 2017, Space Science Reviews, section 3.1 (saved: data/raw/mars_sites/martinez2017_ssr_review.pdf)).
sentences.haze: Earth's ranked squares range in yearly aerosol optical depth from 0.00 (-84.5, -177.5, Transantarctic Mountains) to 0.72 (31.5, 102.5, Tibetan Plateau). North of 60 S the lowest is 0.02 (-50.5, -69.5, Patagonian Desert). The haziest month reaches 1.13 (31.5, 72.5). These are all particles together, not dust alone, rounded to two decimals. Our files give Mars dust optical depth generally below 1 in the aphelion season. At the peak of global dust storms it is above 3 (Mars: Martinez et al. 2017, Space Science Reviews, section 3.1 (saved: data/raw/mars_sites/martinez2017_ssr_review.pdf)). Earth's haziest month is just above that 'below 1', and far from a Mars dust storm.

mars_comparison.rule: Mars figures only as data/derived/mars_sites.json holds them (site cards made from mars_climate.json); 'not in our data' where they do not; nothing typed from memory

mars_power.what: Power on site: how well solar, wind and geothermal power would do at each place, with the Moon and Mars beside it.
mars_power.rough_estimate: A rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement or an engineering study.
rules_in_words: Panel yield, rule of thumb: kWh a day from each kilowatt of panels = sunlight on level ground (kWh per square metre per day) x 0.75. A panel's kilowatt rating assumes 1 kW per square metre of sunlight; 0.75 allows for heat, dirt, snow, wiring and inverter losses. Panels tilted toward the Sun do better at high latitude (a low Sun hits a level panel at a glancing angle); that is not counted here.
Solar class 'good': yearly mean sunlight on level ground of at least 4.5 kWh per square metre per day (about 1,640 kWh per square metre a year).

Solar class 'fair': from 3.0 up to 4.5 kWh per square metre per day; 'poor' below 3.0. These cut values are our own: sunny deserts (5.5 to 7) read good, central Europe (about 3) fair to poor, the high Arctic (about 2) poor.
A month counts as having no sunlight (polar night) when NASA POWER gives exactly 0.0 for it; a month the service leaves blank is unknown (null), not dark.

Sunlight above the air at the distance of Earth and the Moon from the Sun: 1,361 watts per square metre (NASA NSSDCA Earth and Moon fact sheets, saved in this project). At the Moon's south pole a panel standing upright and facing a Sun on the horizon receives all of it, because there is no air.

Air mass at Sun height h (degrees), the thickness of air the sunlight crosses relative to a Sun overhead, by Kasten and Young (1989), Applied Optics 28(22), 4735-4738: AM = 1 / (sin h + 0.50572 x (h + 6.07995)^-1.6364). Sea level; the place's height is not counted.

Direct beam on a panel facing the Sun through clear air, by Meinel and Meinel (1976), Applied Solar Energy (Addison-Wesley), as quoted by PVEducation: beam = 1,361 x 0.7^(AM^0.678) watts per square metre. 0.7 is the share passed by one air mass of typical clear air; the exponent 0.678 allows for air that is not uniform.
The power is worked out at each lunar Sun ceiling (the limit_deg of each region in grazing_cells.json) and at half its height, because the Sun spends much of the low-Sun hours below the ceiling.

A place's clear-sky share in its best ten-day periods = mean of (1 - cloud percent / 100) over the months of the ten-day periods listed in grazing_cells.json under targets.<region>.top_bins, weighted by the low-Sun hours of each period. Cloud percent is cloud_pct of cloud_cells.json (monthly mean over all hours, CERES SYN1deg). The low-Sun power under the place's typical sky = clear-sky figure x that share. Null where the region has no best periods at the place or the cloud is unknown.
Air density at sea level in the International Standard Atmosphere: 1.225 kilograms per cubic metre.

Air density at height z metres (International Standard Atmosphere, lower 11 km): 1.225 x (1 - 0.0065 x z / 288.15)^4.2559. z is the mean height of the model grid box the 50 m wind is given for (as the service names it in each answer); where the service gives no height, sea-level density is used and the height is null. Cold polar air is denser than the standard atmosphere (about 10 % at -15 C), which would raise the figure; that is not counted.

Factor for the usual spread of wind speeds: if speeds follow a Rayleigh distribution the mean of the speed cubed is 6 / pi = 1.91 times the mean speed cubed, which is how the standard 50 m wind classes were tied to mean speeds.

Power in the wind at 50 m = 0.5 x air density x 1.91 x (yearly mean speed)^3, in watts per square metre of rotor area: the power the moving air carries, not what a turbine delivers (a turbine takes at most 59 %, in practice 35 to 45 %). The yearly mean speed is the plain mean of the 12 monthly means of NASA POWER's WS50M.

Wind power classes 1 to 7 at 50 m (US Department of Energy and NREL, Elliott et al. 1986, Wind Energy Resource Atlas of the United States; at sea level these match mean speeds of 5.6, 6.4, 7.0, 7.5, 8.0 and 8.8 m/s): class 1 below 200 W per square metre, 2 from 200, 3 from 300, 4 from 400, 5 from 500, 6 from 600, 7 from 800. The bands are from the published table as we know it; no copy was saved tonight.
Wind class 'good': class 4 or higher (at least 400 watts per square metre at 50 m).
Wind class 'fair': classes 2 and 3 (200 up to 400); 'poor': class 1 (below 200).
Geothermal class 'good': a working geothermal power plant (WRI Global Power Plant Database, primary fuel geothermal) lies within 50 km ...
... or a volcano that erupted since 1990 lies within 30 km.
'Erupted since 1990': the Smithsonian list of volcanoes gives a last eruption year of 1990 or later, or its list of eruptions holds a confirmed eruption that started or ended in 1990 or later.
Geothermal class 'fair': a working geothermal plant within 150 km, or any volcano of the Holocene (the last 11,700 years) within 100 km ...
... 'poor' otherwise.
Distances are along the ground (great circle) from the area or square centre, on a sphere of mean Earth radius 6,371 km.
NASA POWER is asked one request at a time, at least 2 seconds apart.
On a refusal (429) or a server fault (5xx) we back off at least a minute.
On a dropped network we wait 20, 40, 60 ... seconds (at most 300) and try again.

panel_factor.unit: kWh per kW of panels per kWh per m2

density_with_height.unit: lapse K per m, sea-level K, exponent

wind_power_rule.unit: W per m2 of rotor area

mars_power.classes: each part has a class in plain words (good, fair, poor; null where its inputs are unknown) and the figures behind it
mars_power.null_rule: Unknown is null, never 0. A real 0.0 (a month of polar night) stays 0.0.

what_it_is.solar: Sunlight on level ground: NASA POWER ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, all solar energy (direct plus diffuse) reaching a level surface per day under the real sky, monthly mean over the service's years, for the 1 degree box that holds the place (CERES SYN1deg). Yearly mean = plain mean of the 12 months. Panel yield and class by the rules above.
what_it_is.low_sun: Clear-air power on a panel facing a Sun at each lunar Sun ceiling and at half of it, from the air mass of Kasten and Young (1989) and the direct-beam formula of Meinel and Meinel (1976), then times the place's clear-sky share in its best low-Sun ten-day periods.
what_it_is.wind: Mean wind speed 50 m above the ground: NASA POWER WS50M (POWER from the MERRA-2 reanalysis), monthly mean over all hours, at the MERRA-2 grid point nearest the place (0.5 by 0.625 degrees). Power in the wind and class by the rules above. ws10m_ms_year is the 10 m speed of the power-extra group (WS10M), given for comparison.
what_it_is.geothermal: A rule-of-thumb class from what is steadily there: working geothermal power plants (WRI Global Power Plant Database) and volcanoes of the last 11,700 years and those that erupted since 1990 (Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program). The figures behind it: nearest plant with name, size and distance; plants and megawatts within 150 km; nearest volcano erupted since 1990; nearest Holocene volcano.

what_it_is_not.solar: This is not the output of a tilted panel or of a panel that follows the Sun. It is not a measurement at the place, and it is not the light of the hours of low Sun only. The value is for a coarse box of approximately 111 km by 20 to 55 km at these latitudes.
what_it_is_not.low_sun: Not measured; diffuse light from the sky is left out; real polar air (haze, ice crystals, aerosol) varies; cloud is a monthly mean over all hours and a box about 111 km tall, not over the low-Sun hours. This is a textbook clear-air estimate: real polar air and haze vary from day to day, so a real panel can get less or somewhat more; it shows that Earth's low Sun delivers only a fraction of the power the same low Sun gives a panel on the Moon, where no air stands in the way.
what_it_is_not.wind: A coarse grid mean (a box of about 55 km by 20 to 35 km here), not a measurement at the place: local hills, coasts, valleys, ice slopes (katabatic winds) and icing of the blades change it greatly. Not what a turbine would deliver.
what_it_is_not.geothermal: This class does not come from a drill hole or from a heat measurement here. It only says that hot rock is probably near the surface. A place far from volcanoes can also have useful warm ground (deep basins, hot springs), and a place near a volcano can be unusable. For this version of the page, we did not find an open map of geothermal potential for the world that is available without a login. The list of plants stops in approximately 2021 and does not include some plants.

notes_from_the_sanity_look: Sunlight comes in 1 degree boxes. Yungay in the Atacama (square m_-24.25_-70.25) lies at the east edge of a box that reaches about 80 km out over the Pacific and its coastal cloud deck, so it reads 5.96 kWh per m2 per day; the next box inland (square m_-24.25_-69.75) reads 7.21, close to the highest in the file (7.38, on the Altiplano).

The highest 50 m winds (yearly means of 17 to 19 m/s) are on the coastal slopes of East Antarctica, where the MERRA-2 model's katabatic winds run strong; the 10 m wind of the same model is nearly as high there. Model values, not checked against stations; blades there would also face extreme gusts and icing.
High ground has thin air: on the Tibetan Plateau (grid height about 5 km) the same mean wind carries about 40 % less power than at sea level, a small step toward Mars, where it carries about 1 %.
Geothermal 'poor' does not mean no warm ground: Tibet has a working plant (Yangbajain) 400 km from our square and many hot springs without volcanoes, which this rule does not see.

t2m_range_c.service_definition: The difference between the minimum and maximum hourly air (dry bulb) temperature at 2 meters above the surface of the earth in the period of interest.
t2m_range_c.grid: MERRA-2 grid, 0.5 degree of latitude by 0.625 degree of longitude (about 55 km by 15 to 35 km at these latitudes); each place takes the nearest grid point (grid_merra2)
t2m_range_c.what_it_is: Mean daily swing of air temperature 2 m above the ground: the day's warmest hour minus its coldest hour, averaged over the days of each calendar month, in degrees C. A model value (MERRA-2 reanalysis, worked out by POWER from hourly values) for the grid point nearest the place. Checked on this run against the daily series of six grid points kept by the temperature group: it equals the mean of the daily ranges of 2001 to 2020 (see t2m_range_check).
t2m_range_c.what_it_is_not: Not a measurement at the place and not the ground's own swing (the ground's surface swings more than the air above it). Not the swing on a clear day (it is an average over all days, cloudy ones included), not the range between the month's extremes, and not the swing during the hours of low Sun. A mean over a grid box at the box's own mean height, which near an ice cap or a mountain coast lies far from the place.
t2m_range_c.year_field: t2m_range_c_year: the service's annual value (ANN), as given; it lies within a few hundredths of the plain mean of the 12 months shown (see annual_check)

albedo.service_definition: The all sky rate of reflectivity of the earth's surface; the ratio of the solar energy reflected by the surface of the earth compared to the total solar energy incident reaching the surface of the earth.
albedo.grid: CERES SYN1deg grid, 1 degree boxes (about 111 km tall); each place takes the box that holds it (grid_ceres); polewards of 45 degrees neighbouring boxes along a latitude often carry the same value (see albedo_repeat_check)
albedo.what_it_is: Surface albedo: the share of the sunlight reaching the ground that the ground sends back, 0 to 1, as a mean for each calendar month under the real sky (all sky, clouds included). It is the brightness of whatever covers the ground in that month, snow and ice included, over a coarse grid box of 1 degree (CERES SYN1deg as served by POWER). Null in months the service gives no value (no sunlight: polar night).
albedo.what_it_is_not: Not the colour or brightness of the bare rock at the place: a box of about 111 km by 20 to 110 km mixes rock, snow, ice, water and plants, and in the months when snow lies it is mostly the snow. Not a measurement at the place, and not the albedo of the ground at low Sun angles alone. Low-Sun months near the polar night rest on few hours of sunlight and are the least sure. Not comparable as-is with lunar albedo figures, which are measured another way (often at one wavelength and one viewing angle).
albedo.year_field: albedo_year: the service's annual value (ANN), as given: close to the plain mean of the months that have a value, so near the poles a mean over the sunlit months only, not weighted by sunlight (see annual_check)

soil_wetness_top.service_definition: The amount of water and water vapor present in the soil. Top indicates the upper 5 cm of soil. Values range from 0 for completely dry conditions to 1 for completely saturated soil.
soil_wetness_top.grid: MERRA-2 grid, 0.5 degree of latitude by 0.625 degree of longitude (about 55 km by 15 to 35 km at these latitudes); each place takes the nearest grid point (grid_merra2)
soil_wetness_top.what_it_is: Surface soil wetness of the top 5 cm: a model value from 0 (completely dry) to 1 (saturated), monthly mean, from the MERRA-2 land model (reanalysis) at the grid point nearest the place.
soil_wetness_top.what_it_is_not: Not a measurement: a model value, not a probe in the ground, and not a percent of water by volume. Near the poles and on high plateaus the top layer is frozen or under snow for much of the year; how the model counts frozen water was not checked on this run, so winter values say nothing sure about liquid water or dust. A grid box mixes the place with its surroundings, glaciers and wetlands included. Where the model's grid point is ice (glacier, ice sheet) it gives 1.00 in every month: that is the model's ice, not wet soil, and soil_wetness_ice_flag is true there (even where the place itself is bare rock, such as the McMurdo Dry Valleys).
soil_wetness_top.year_field: soil_wetness_top_year: the service's annual value (ANN), as given; it lies within a few hundredths of the plain mean of the 12 months shown (see annual_check)

wind_10m_ms.service_definition: The average of wind speed at 10 meters above the surface of the earth.
wind_10m_ms.grid: MERRA-2 grid, 0.5 degree of latitude by 0.625 degree of longitude (about 55 km by 15 to 35 km at these latitudes); each place takes the nearest grid point (grid_merra2)
wind_10m_ms.what_it_is: Mean wind speed 10 m above the ground, in metres per second, averaged over all hours of each calendar month: a model value (MERRA-2 reanalysis, served by POWER) at the grid point nearest the place.
wind_10m_ms.what_it_is_not: Not a measurement at the place and not the wind a person or a rover would meet at the ground (at 1 to 2 m the wind is slower, behind a ridge it can be far slower, in a gap or at the foot of an ice slope far faster). Not gusts, not the strongest wind of the month and not the wind direction. A mean over a grid box of tens of kilometres with smoothed hills, so it misses valley and katabatic winds smaller than the box.
wind_10m_ms.year_field: wind_10m_ms_year: the service's annual value (ANN), as given; it lies within a few hundredths of the plain mean of the 12 months shown (see annual_check)

grid_fields.grid_merra2: [lat, lon] of the MERRA-2 grid point the temperature range, soil wetness and wind speed were read at (nearest to the place centre)
grid_fields.grid_ceres: [lat, lon] of the centre of the 1 degree box the albedo was read at
grid_fields.soil_wetness_ice_flag: true when the top-soil wetness is 0.995 or more in all 12 months: the model's grid point is ice, so the soil wetness says nothing about soil there; false otherwise; null when unknown

t2m_range_check.how: for each daily series on disk (data/raw/power_temperature/daily_points/, NASA POWER daily point API, T2M_MAX and T2M_MIN of each day, 2001 to 2025), the mean of (T2M_MAX - T2M_MIN) by calendar month over 2001-2020 and over 2001-2025, against this file's T2M_RANGE of the same grid point

mars_rock_frozen.what_this_is: For every place: the main rock class of the half-degree box around it (GLiM) and the modelled permafrost probability and zone (Obu et al. 2019, north of 25 N only). Context beside the light ranking, not part of it.

what_it_is.rock.class: The main rock class (GLiM first level, 16 classes) of a half-degree box, about 55 km north-south, in plain words. It is the class a geological map compilation gives most of that box.
what_it_is.rock.volcanic: yes when the class is basic, intermediate or acid volcanic rock, or pyroclastic rock
what_it_is.rock.basic_volcanic: yes when the class is basic volcanic rock (basalt and the like)
what_it_is.rock.loose_sediment: yes when the class is unconsolidated sediment (loose sand, gravel, silt, clay)
what_it_is.rock.box: 'own' = the box that holds the place; 'neighbour' = that box is sea or no data, so the most common rock class of the 8 boxes around it is given
what_it_is.rock.box_sw: south-west corner (lat, lon, degrees) of the half-degree box the class belongs to
what_it_is.permafrost.prob_mean: Mean modelled permafrost probability (fraction 0-1) of the 1 km pixels under the sample points that have a map value. Obu et al. model mean annual ground temperature at the top of the permafrost for 2000-2016; the probability is the share of their model runs with it below 0 C.
what_it_is.permafrost.zone: Zone of the MEAN, by Obu et al.'s limits: continuous >= 0.9, discontinuous 0.5-0.9, sporadic 0.1-0.5, isolated patches above 0 and under 0.1, none = 0.
what_it_is.permafrost.points / points_with_value: sample points in the place / those on a pixel with a value; the rest fall on sea, lakes, glaciers or ice sheets, which the map leaves empty, or in its gaps (most of the Sahara and much of Arabia between 25 and 30 N have no value although they are land)
what_it_is.permafrost.share_points_ge_half: share of the points with a value whose probability is 0.5 or more

what_it_is_not.rock: Not the rock at the place. One class per 55 km box; small outcrops, a single hill or the ground of an 11 km area can be another rock. There is NO class for anorthosite (the bright rock of the Moon's highlands and of the south-pole landing regions): anorthosite bodies on Earth are inside the plutonic or metamorphic classes. 'Basic volcanic' is the closest the map comes to the Moon's mare basalts, which are not at the candidate regions. 'Ice and glaciers' means the map does not say what rock lies under or between the ice; the three yes-or-no fields are then null, not no.
what_it_is_not.permafrost: Not a measurement in the ground: a 1 km model, validated against boreholes with an error of about 2 C in ground temperature. Not the depth of thaw in summer (the active layer) and not ice content. The zone is the zone of the area's mean, not of every pixel; an 'isolated patches' area can hold no permafrost at all on the ground. Glaciers, ice sheets and water have no value; a place mostly under ice gets few points or none.
what_it_is_not.mars_permafrost: nine points in a 55 km square: a thin sample of nine 1 km pixels, not an area mean
what_it_is_not.antarctica: Not in our data. The Obu et al. Northern Hemisphere map covers land from 25 N northward only and does not cover Antarctica; the literature says ice-free ground in Antarctica is permafrost throughout. The fields are null with that note.

fields.median_slope_deg: The median slope in degrees. Each slope covers approximately 3.7 km, and the heights are 1.85 km apart. On Earth, the median uses the land of the square (0.5 degree, approximately 55 km from north to south). On Mars, it uses the 2 x 2 degree box of the site (approximately 118 km).
fields.p90_slope_deg: The 90th percentile of the slopes, over the same span as the median slope.
fields.relief_m: The 95th percentile of the heights minus the 5th percentile, in metres, over the square or the box of the site.
fields.relief_class: a band of relief_m (table relief_classes), over 55 km squares or 118 km boxes
fields.slope_pixels: pixels with a slope (about 1.85 km each)

relief_classes.class: very high relief (915 m or more)

is_not: No roughness at 90, 270 or 810 m and no landform class: a height every 1.85 km cannot see them, and the Moon part's landform table was set for 10 km windows of 90 m pixels; its slope thresholds would put almost every square in 'plain' at a 3.7 km span. Both are null by design, not unknown by accident.
No terrain shadow: the Mars part has no Sun table by sector and Sun height and no horizon file.
A Mars site box (118 km) is about twice an Earth square (55 km north-south, narrower east-west), so their reliefs are not over the same area.
Slopes over 3.7 km are much gentler than slopes a rover or a person meets.

mars_hazards_people.place_point: the square centre (lat and lon of the square's record in mars_cells.json); a square is half a degree (about 55 km north-south, less east-west away from the equator), so a distance from any point of it differs by up to about 40 km, and a 100 or 200 km circle from the centre is not the square
mars_hazards_people.what_this_is: For every place: earthquakes of magnitude 5 and above within 200 km (1990-2025), the nearest volcano of the Holocene list, and the settlements nearby. Facts from three public lists, measured from the place's centre along the great circle; read beside the light ranking, not part of it.

what_this_is_not.quakes_m5_200km: This is not a hazard map and not a forecast. It counts the earthquakes of magnitude 5 and above in the USGS catalogue from 1 January 1990 to 31 December 2025. Each epicentre is within 200 km of the centre of the place. These are 36 years of a catalogue, not the ground motion that a site can expect. The count does not include smaller earthquakes, which people can still feel. It does not use depth: a deep earthquake 200 km away counts the same as a shallow one. The magnitudes are the preferred values of the catalogue, of mixed types (mw, mb, ms, ...), thus 'magnitude 5' is not one scale everywhere. The count does not include events that the catalogue gives a type other than 'earthquake' (nuclear explosions, volcanic eruptions, a mine collapse, a landslide).
what_this_is_not.volcano: Not a hazard map and not a forecast. It is the straight-line distance from the place's centre to the listed position (one point, usually the summit or the centre of a volcanic field) of the nearest volcano in the Smithsonian list of Holocene volcanoes. A volcanic field or a fissure system can reach far from its point. 'Last eruption year' is the list's own field (negative = BCE); null means the list gives none, which is common for volcanoes whose Holocene activity is uncertain or undated, not that the volcano never erupted. Pleistocene volcanoes (older than ~11,700 years) are not in the list.
what_this_is_not.people: Straight-line distance, not travel time: no road, sea, ice or border is considered. A list of settlements, not a population map: GeoNames cities1000 lists places with more than 1,000 people plus seats of administrative divisions down to the third level; settlements under 1,000 people (most Arctic and many desert camps, all Antarctic stations) are not in it, so 'no settlement within 100 km' does not mean nobody lives there. 'Population within 100 km' is the sum of the populations the list gives for the settlements whose point lies within 100 km: a whole town counts if its point is inside, none of it if outside; the figures are of mixed years; a municipality's figure can cover land far from its point; listed places with no population figure are counted apart (settlements_without_population_within_100km), never as 0. City sections (PPLX) and abandoned, destroyed or historical places are left out.

mars_hazards_people.distance: great circle on a sphere of radius 6371.0 km (haversine); against the real ellipsoid within about 0.5 percent
mars_hazards_people.search: a grid index (cells of 1 degree, 2 degrees for the volcanoes) narrows the candidates; every kept point is decided by its great-circle distance, and the nearest-point search widens until it finds one, up to the whole globe, so no distance is capped

mars_steady_effects.place_point: the square centre (lat and lon in mars_cells.json); a square is half a degree (about 55 km north-south) so the 2, 5, 10 and 25 km tests describe only the middle of the square
mars_steady_effects.what_this_is: For every place: what volcanoes and people steadily do there (not the risk of a rare event), with the useful side of each (young volcanic ground; help within reach), and a small-tremor class (the catalogue's verdict where it can see small tremors, our rough estimate where it cannot). Read beside the light ranking, not part of it.
mars_steady_effects.rule_of_thumb: This is a rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement.
rules_in_plain_words: This is a rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement.

volcanic, 'steady volcanic effects likely': a volcano that erupted in 3 or more separate years since 1990, or at any time since 2015, lies within 30 km of the place's centre. What it means for the work: gas and volcanic haze that can corrode and fog instruments and optics; fine ash and abrasive dust on the ground and in the air; warm or steaming ground that upsets temperature readings; small volcanic tremors; closures of the area when it erupts.

volcanic, 'volcanic effects come and go': a volcano that erupted since 1990 lies within 100 km. What it means for the work: gas and volcanic haze that can corrode and fog instruments and optics; fine ash and abrasive dust on the ground and in the air; warm or steaming ground that upsets temperature readings; small volcanic tremors; closures of the area when it erupts.

volcanic, 'young volcanic ground (useful side, yes or no)': yes when a Holocene volcano (active in the last ~11,700 years, any date) lies within 50 km and the rock map (data/derived/rock_frozen_cells.json or mars_rock_frozen.json, when present) calls the place's rock volcanic; no when there is no such volcano within 50 km or the rock map says the rock is not volcanic; null when a volcano is that close but the rock map gives no class. Fresh lava and ash are a good stand-in for the basalt soil of the Moon's dark plains and of Mars.

human, 'steady human disturbance likely': a listed settlement of 1,000 or more people lies within 5 km, or a main road or railway within 2 km, or an airfield with scheduled flights within 10 km. What it means for the work: vibration from vehicles and aircraft; radio noise; dust raised by traffic; artificial light; tracks and litter in camera views.

human, 'human disturbance possible': a listed settlement of any size lies within 25 km, or a main road or railway within 10 km, or an airfield of any kind within 10 km. What it means for the work: vibration from vehicles and aircraft; radio noise; dust raised by traffic; artificial light; tracks and litter in camera views.
human, 'undisturbed as far as our lists show': otherwise.

human, 'help within reach (useful side, yes or no)': yes when a listed settlement of 1,000 or more lies within 50 km or an airfield with scheduled flights within 100 km (power, shelter, rescue); no otherwise.
small tremors, 'small tremors likely': a volcano that erupted since 1990 lies within 50 km, or at least 5 earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more were catalogued within 200 km since 1990.

small tremors, 'small tremors possible': a Holocene volcano of any date lies within 100 km, or 1 to 4 earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more within 200 km since 1990, or glacier ice covers 10% or more of the area's land (moving ice makes small quakes).

rules.when: If a volcano within 30 km of the centre erupted in 3 or more separate years since 1990, steady volcanic effects are likely. If such a volcano erupted at any time since 2015, they are also likely.
what_the_effects_are: gas and volcanic haze that can corrode and fog instruments and optics
fine ash and abrasive dust on the ground and in the air
warm or steaming ground that upsets temperature readings
small volcanic tremors
closures of the area when it erupts

rules.when: If a volcano within 100 km erupted since 1990, volcanic effects come and go.
what_the_effects_are: gas and volcanic haze that can corrode and fog instruments and optics
fine ash and abrasive dust on the ground and in the air
warm or steaming ground that upsets temperature readings
small volcanic tremors
closures of the area when it erupts

Fresh lava and ash are a good stand-in for the basalt soil of the Moon's dark plains and of Mars

If a listed settlement of 1,000 or more people is within 5 km, steady human disturbance is likely. The same class applies if a main road or railway is within 2 km, or if an airfield with scheduled flights is within 10 km.

radio noise
dust raised by traffic
artificial light
tracks and litter in camera views

rules.when: If a listed settlement of any size is within 25 km, human disturbance is possible. The same class applies if a main road or railway is within 10 km, or if an airfield of any kind is within 10 km.
what_the_effects_are: vibration from vehicles and aircraft
radio noise
dust raised by traffic
artificial light
tracks and litter in camera views

rules.outcome: undisturbed as far as our lists show
rules.when: This class applies if no other rule of its group applies.

rules.outcome: help within reach (useful side, yes or no)
rules.when: yes when a listed settlement of 1,000 or more lies within 50 km or an airfield with scheduled flights within 100 km (power, shelter, rescue); no otherwise
a volcano that erupted since 1990 lies within 50 km, or at least 5 earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more were catalogued within 200 km since 1990

a Holocene volcano of any date lies within 100 km, or 1 to 4 earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more within 200 km since 1990, or glacier ice covers 10% or more of the area's land (moving ice makes small quakes)
This class applies if no other rule of its group applies.

rules_left_out_here: small tremors: the glacier-ice part of the 'possible' test is left out for the Mars squares, which have no ice share in the project's files

volcanic.class: one of the three classes of the rules
volcanic.effects: the fixed list of what a steady or recurring volcanic presence does to field work; the same words for every place of the class, not observed at the place; empty for 'none expected'
volcanic.decided_by: the volcano that set the class (the nearest one meeting the class's test), or null
volcanic.nearest_erupted_since_1990: the nearest volcano with a confirmed eruption in progress in 1990 or later, any distance: name, GVP number, km, the number of separate calendar years since 1990 with an eruption in progress, the last such year, and whether the list says it is still going on
volcanic.nearest_holocene: the nearest volcano of the Holocene list, any date (it can be the same volcano)
volcanic.young_volcanic_ground: true, false or null by the rule; the useful side, kept apart from the class
volcanic.rock_map_volcanic: the rock map's own yes/no (null when it gives none), copied from the rock file
volcanic.is_not: Not a hazard map, not an eruption forecast. A volcano is one listed point (summit or field centre); a fissure system or field can reach well beyond it, and gas or ash can drift much farther than 100 km downwind. 'Years erupting' counts calendar years in which the list has a confirmed eruption in progress: an eruption with no end year counts its start year only; uncertain and discredited eruptions are left out; lava lakes and steady degassing between listed eruptions are not counted (a volcano can steam and smell for decades between them).

human.class: one of the three classes of the rules
human.why: which of the class's tests held, in words
human.effects: the fixed list of what steady human presence does to field work; empty when undisturbed
human.nearest_settlement: nearest listed settlement (GeoNames cities1000), its population (null when the list gives none) and km
human.nearest_settlement_1000_or_more: nearest listed settlement whose listed population is 1,000 or more
human.population_within_25km: The sum of the listed populations of the settlements with a point within 25 km. The value is 0 if no settlement is listed. It is unknown if settlements are listed but none has a figure. It is a lower bound if only some settlements have no figure.
human.nearest_main_road_or_railway: the nearest Natural Earth 1:10m road or railway (ferry routes left out), with its class, type, name and km; km null and none_within_km 1000 when there is none that close
human.nearest_airfield: nearest runway airfield of any size (OurAirports small, medium or large airport, gravel and ice strips included; heliports, seaplane bases and closed fields left out, as in data/derived/access_cells.json), with km
human.nearest_airfield_with_scheduled_flights: the same, among airfields the table flags as having scheduled service
human.help_within_reach: true or false by the rule; the useful side, kept apart from the class
human.is_not: This is not a population map, and it is not a measurement of noise or light. Each distance is a straight line, not a travel distance. GeoNames cities1000 lists places of more than 1,000 people and seats of local government, thus camps, stations, mines and hamlets are not in the list. Natural Earth holds only main roads and railways. Thus, if a road is not in the data, this does not prove that there is no road. Most tracks, winter roads and mine roads are not in the data. We know only that an airfield exists, not its traffic.

small_tremors.class: the catalogue's verdict from the tremors file where it has one, else our estimate
small_tremors.catalogue_verdict: the verdict of data/derived/tremors_cells.json (or mars_tremors.json), null if the file or the place is missing
small_tremors.our_estimate: our rule's class, worked out for every place so it can be compared where the catalogue sees
small_tremors.m5_quakes_200km_since_1990: earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more within 200 km, 1990-2025, from the hazards file (null if the file is missing)
small_tremors.glacier_ice_share: share of the area's land mapped as snow and ice (ESA WorldCover in the north; the south's ice-sheet share), from the landcover files; null for the Mars squares
small_tremors.is_not: Not a count and not a measurement of small tremors: a guess from what usually makes them (active volcanoes, a seismically busy region, moving glaciers). Small tremors can occur where it says unlikely, and need not occur where it says likely.

mars_steady_effects.distance: great circle on a sphere of radius 6371.0 km (haversine); against the real ellipsoid within about 0.5 percent

distance_check.how: one degree along the equator = pi x 6371 / 180
equator to pole = a quarter of the circumference
across the North Pole, 0.5 degree each side
60N to 60N over the pole = 60 degrees of arc

mars_steady_effects.search: grid indexes (1 degree cells; 0.5 degree for road and rail points); every kept point is decided by its great-circle distance; nearest searches widen until they find a point (roads and railways: up to 1000 km)
mars_steady_effects.roads_accuracy: points added along every road and railway so none is more than 1.5 km from the next; the distance to the nearest point overstates the distance to the line by at most 0.75 km. Natural Earth 1:10m lines are themselves generalised (often a kilometre or more off the real road)

query.spans: Moon: months north of 55 N, years south of 55 S; Mars: quarters worldwide; any answer refused as over 20,000 events was asked again by month, then by halves of longitude
query.event_types: all types the catalogue lists (earthquakes, quarry blasts, explosions, ice quakes and others); duplicates across spans removed by event id
query.raw_answers: data/raw/usgs_small_quakes/mars/ (manifest.json lists each URL, its row count and when it was fetched)

mars_tremors.magnitude_range: 2.5 up to (not including) 5.0, any magnitude type, as the catalogue gives it

rule_of_thumb.words: This is our own rule, not an engineering standard. The class is 'steady small tremors' if catalogued events occurred within 100 km in at least 12 of the 16 years. The rate must also be at least 5 a year. The class is 'occasional small tremors' if at least one event occurred within 100 km, but not steadily. That is, in 1 to 11 of the years, or less than 5 a year. Events in 1 to 3 years are usually a single swarm. The class is 'none recorded' if the catalogue records small tremors here and has no event within 100 km. The class is 'cannot tell' if the catalogue cannot see small tremors here. It is also 'cannot tell' if the catalogue sees only tremors above a magnitude between 2.5 and 3.5 and has no event within 100 km. Then an empty circle tells nothing about smaller tremors.
rule_of_thumb.status_words: The detection floor is the 10th percentile of the magnitudes of all catalogued events from 2.5 to under 5 within 500 km over the 16 years (null if fewer than 30 events). Only magnitude 2.5 and up was fetched here, so the floor cannot be read below 2.5; a floor under 2.6 is read as 'at or below 2.5'. 'small tremors are recorded here' when the floor is at or below 2.5; 'only tremors of magnitude M and above are recorded here' when it is above 2.5 and at most 3.5; 'small tremors cannot be seen in this catalogue here' when it is above 3.5 or there are too few events to tell. A floor at or below 2.5 counts only if the catalogue also lists at least one event under that magnitude within 200 km of the place (field floor_check); otherwise the low floor is borrowed from a better-watched network farther away, as western Alaska seen from Chukotka or Texas seen from Coahuila, and the place is read as 'cannot be seen'. Where small tremors cannot be seen the counts are null, never 0: no record is not the same as no tremors.

fields.small_per_year_50km: The mean number of catalogued events a year, of magnitude 2.5 to less than 5, within 50 km of the centre of the place, 2010-2025. If the catalogue cannot see small tremors here, the value is unknown.
fields.years_with_events_100km: The number of years, of the 16 years, with at least one such event in the catalogue within 100 km. This number shows if the events are consistent: 14 of 16 is steady, and 1 of 16 is one swarm. If the catalogue cannot see small tremors here, the value is unknown.
fields.median_magnitude_100km: median magnitude of those events within 100 km (null if none)
fields.largest_small_magnitude_100km: largest magnitude among them, always under 5 (null if none)
fields.nearest_small_event_km: distance to the nearest catalogued event of magnitude 2.5 to under 5, searched out to 500 km (null if none that close)
fields.share_not_earthquake_100km: share of the events within 100 km that the catalogue types as something other than an earthquake (quarry blast, explosion, ice quake and so on); these shake instruments too and are counted
fields.events_500km_for_floor: how many catalogued events of magnitude 2.5 to under 5 lie within 500 km: the sample the floor is read from
fields.detection_floor: estimated smallest magnitude the catalogue reliably records in this region: the 10th percentile of the magnitudes within 500 km (null if fewer than 30 events)
fields.floor_check: 'passed' or 'failed: ...' where the floor was at or below the 'recorded' line: whether at least one event under it is catalogued within 200 km; a failed check turns the status to 'cannot be seen' (null where the check does not apply)
fields.catalogued_anyway_100km: only where small tremors cannot be seen: the events the catalogue still lists within 100 km (count, years, smallest magnitude), mostly magnitude 4 and up; a sign of activity and a lower bound, not a rate of small tremors (null otherwise)
fields.verdict: plain verdict for instruments, by the rule of thumb in meta.rule_of_thumb

mars_tremors.what_it_is_not: A count of catalogued events, not a measurement of ground motion at the place; not a hazard map; a seismometer on site is the only real test. The catalogue lists only what nearby seismometers detected, so its reach differs by region: in Alaska it sees magnitude 1 to 2, in the remote Arctic, Siberia and Antarctica almost nothing under 4. The networks also grew during the 16 years (north of 55 N the catalogue lists about 1.6 times as many events of magnitude 1 to 5 a year in 2017-2025 as in 2010-2015; in some places, such as the Kobuk valley, several times as many), so early years undercount and 'years with events' leans low. Distances are from the place centre.
mars_tremors.grid_index: events in 1-degree bins; each search reads only the bins that can reach the circle, then measures great-circle distance
mars_tremors.edge_note: Only magnitude 2.5 and up was fetched worldwide, so 'small' here means 2.5 to under 5 and the Mars squares cannot be compared one to one with the Moon areas (magnitude 1 and up).

mars_estimates.what: Rough estimates, by our own stated rules, for seven factors that have no open Earth data, for every place of the Mars part (the squares of data/derived/mars_cells.json).
mars_estimates.sentence: This is a rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement.

rules.name: Snow-free months (used by rules 2, 4 and 6)
rules.rule: These are the calendar months with a mean air temperature above 0 C at 2 m above the ground, in the NASA POWER grid. The Moon part uses temperature_cells.json, and the Mars part uses mars_climate.json. If no month is above 0 C, the rule uses the warmest month only. The rule uses temperature, not the snow maps, to make sure that the Moon part and the Mars part use the same rule.
rules.classes: a list of month numbers, 1 = January
rules.note: This is a rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement.

rules.name: Rockiness
rules.rule: The class is high if three conditions are true. At least 0.5 of the land is bare. The ground is steep or rough. The rock map does not say loose sediment. Steep or rough means a 90th-percentile slope of 10 degrees or more. It can also mean a roughness at 90 m that is not less than that of the smoothest lunar region. The class is low if less than 0.25 of the land is bare. It is also low if the rock map says loose sediment and the 90th-percentile slope is less than 5 degrees. If not, the class is medium. The Mars part has no roughness at 90 m, thus only the slope test decides if the ground is steep or rough. Its slopes cover approximately 3.7 km, thus they show flatter ground than the 90 m slopes of the Moon part.
rules.note: This is a rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement.

rules.name: How fast the ground heats and cools
rules.rule: index = the mean of (1 - albedo), divided by the mean daily temperature swing of the air at 2 m. Both means use the snow-free months where both values are known. The unit is 1 per degree C. The index divides the places of each output file into thirds. The lowest third gets 'heats and cools fast, like dry dust or sand'. The middle third gets 'in between'. The highest third gets 'slow, like rock or wet ground'. Both inputs come from coarse climate grids (NASA POWER: CERES 1 degree albedo, MERRA-2 air temperature swing), not from the ground at the place.
rules.note: This is a rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement.

rules.stands_in_for: mineralogy, spectral match and silicate composition
rules.name: Mineral family
rules.rule: One table (meta.mineral_family_table) gives the family from the class of the rock map. Basic volcanic rock gives 'basalt minerals (plagioclase, pyroxene, olivine): like the Moon's dark plains and like Mars'. A place on a listed anorthosite body (data/reference/anorthosite_bodies.json) gives 'plagioclase-rich: like the Moon's bright highlands', with the listed feldspar composition of the body (An number). This result has priority over the class of the map. Each other class gets its usual minerals in a few plain words. For boxes with ice, water or no data, the value is unknown. The rule reads a rock map, not spectra.
rules.note: This is a rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement.

rules.name: Water in the top soil
rules.rule: The class is dry, moist or wet, by thirds of the mean top-soil wetness over the snow-free months (NASA POWER GWETTOP, 0 dry to 1 saturated). The thirds come from the places of each output file (the cut values are in meta.cuts). If the grid point of the model is ice (soil_wetness_ice_flag), the value is unknown. Ground ice is likely if the mean permafrost probability is 0.5 or more, possible from 0.1 to less than 0.5, and unlikely below 0.1. In Antarctica, ground ice is likely, from the literature note of rock_frozen_cells.json (not a map value). If the map has no value and the yearly mean air temperature is 3 C or more, ground ice is unlikely. In other places without a map value, the value is unknown.
rules.classes: dry, moist, wet; ground ice likely, possible, unlikely
rules.note: This is a rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement.

rules.name: Depth to frozen ground
rules.rule: The class comes from the permafrost zone: continuous -> shallow; discontinuous -> shallow in most of the area; sporadic -> patchy; isolated patches -> rare; none -> none expected; Antarctica -> shallow (literature). If the map has no value and the yearly mean air temperature is 3 C or more, the class is none expected (as in rule 4). In other places without a map value, the value is unknown. The rule gives classes only, not metres. The open pages that we read gave no simple rule for each zone for the thickness of the layer that thaws in summer (meta.frozen_ground_depth_sources).
rules.classes: shallow, shallow in most of the area, patchy, rare, none expected, shallow (literature)
rules.note: This is a rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement.

rules.name: Sand and dust on the move
rules.rule: The class is likely if three conditions are true. The ground is loose sediment (rock map) or mostly bare (bare share 0.5 or more). The top soil is in the dry third. The mean wind at 10 m over the snow-free months is 6 m/s or more. The class is unlikely if the top soil is in the wet third, or if the ground is frozen. Frozen means that the grid point of the model is ice, or that the rock map says ice and glaciers. The class is also unlikely if the ground is mostly not bare (bare share less than 0.25: plants, ice or water). If not, the class is possible.
rules.note: This is a rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement.

rules.name: Ilmenite-bearing rock possible
rules.rule: The class is possible if the rock map says basic volcanic rock, or if the place is on a listed anorthosite body. Deposits of iron-titanium oxide occur in both. If not, the class is unlikely. If the map says ice, water or no data and no body is listed, the value is unknown.
rules.note: This is a rough estimate by our own rule. It is not a measurement.

cuts.heat_index_reading: below the first value: fast; from the first to below the second: medium; the second or more: slow (thirds of the Mars-part squares with a value)
cuts.soil_wetness_reading: below the first value: dry; from the first to below the second: moist; the second or more: wet (thirds of the Mars-part squares whose grid point is not ice)

anorthosite.reads: plagioclase-rich: like the Moon's bright highlands

vb.reads: basalt minerals (plagioclase, pyroxene, olivine): like the Moon's dark plains and like Mars

pb.reads: the minerals of basalt (plagioclase, pyroxene, olivine) in coarse crystals (gabbro): close in minerals to the Moon's dark plains and to Mars, not in grain size

vi.reads: plagioclase with pyroxene and amphibole (andesite): unlike the Moon; a little like some Mars rock

pi.reads: plagioclase, amphibole and some quartz (diorite): unlike the Moon and Mars

va.reads: quartz, alkali feldspar and plagioclase (rhyolite, dacite): unlike the Moon and Mars

pa.reads: quartz, alkali feldspar and mica (granite): unlike the Moon and Mars

py.reads: volcanic glass and ash whose make-up varies: unlike the Moon's rock; Mars has ash-like deposits

mt.reads: quartz, feldspar and mica, often with garnet or amphibole (gneiss, schist): unlike the Moon and Mars

ss.reads: grains of quartz, feldspar and clay (sandstone, siltstone, shale): unlike the Moon; Mars has some sandstone and mudstone

sm.reads: quartz, clay and calcite in mixed layers: unlike the Moon; partly like Mars sedimentary rock

sc.reads: calcite and dolomite (limestone, dolomite): unlike the Moon; carbonate is rare on Mars

ev.reads: halite and gypsum (rock salt): unlike the Moon; Mars has sulfate and chloride salt deposits

su.reads: loose grains of quartz, feldspar and clay of mixed make-up: unlike lunar soil in minerals; Mars soil is mostly basalt grains

heat_response_reads.fast: heats and cools fast, like dry dust or sand
heat_response_reads.slow: slow, like rock or wet ground

continuous.reads: frozen ground under the summer-thawed top layer almost everywhere

discontinuous.estimate: shallow in most of the area
discontinuous.reads: frozen ground under the summer-thawed top layer in half to nine-tenths of the area, none in the rest

sporadic.reads: frozen ground in patches only (a tenth to half of the area)

isolated patches.reads: frozen ground only in rare patches (under a tenth of the area)

antarctic literature.reads: ice-free ground in Antarctica is permafrost throughout, by the literature: frozen ground under the summer-thawed top layer; not our map

mars_estimates.water_sentence: Dry soil on Earth holds much more water than lunar soil. Lunar Prospector gives approximately 107 to 158 ppm of hydrogen at the 16 lunar regions (planet_factors.json). If all of this hydrogen is in water, the lunar soil holds only approximately 0.10 to 0.14 % water by weight. A top-soil wetness of 0.1 is approximately 4 % water by volume in a soil with 40 % pore space.

what_it_is_not.rockiness: This is not a count of rocks or boulders, and it is not a rock abundance of the Diviner type. The 90 m height data of Earth cannot see single rocks. The slopes and the roughness are for a window of 10 km (Moon part) or a square of 55 km (Mars part). The rock map gives one class for a box of approximately 55 km.
what_it_is_not.heat_response: This is not thermal inertia. The swing is that of the air 2 m above the ground, in a MERRA-2 grid box of approximately 55 km. The albedo is that of a CERES box of 1 degree. Cloud, humidity, wind and the sea decrease the swing as much as the ground does. Thus a place on a coast can read 'slow' because of the sea, not because of the rock. The thirds are relative to the places of the same file.
what_it_is_not.mineral_family: This does not come from spectra, and it is not an analysis of a sample. It gives the usual minerals of the rock-map class for a box of approximately 55 km, or of a listed anorthosite body. The map has no anorthosite class. Thus the rule misses bodies that are not on our list.
what_it_is_not.topsoil_water: This is not a hydrogen content and not a percent of water. It is a model wetness (0 dry to 1 saturated) of the top 5 cm in a MERRA-2 grid box. The rule divides it into thirds relative to the places of the same file. Ground ice comes from a 1 km model of permafrost probability, not from a borehole.
what_it_is_not.frozen_ground_depth: This is not a depth. It is a class from the permafrost zone only, with no metres. The thaw depth changes from metre to metre with soil, water and plants.
what_it_is_not.sand_dust: This is not an observation of dunes that move or of dust storms. The wind is a monthly mean at 10 m, not the gusts that move sand. If sand moves or not depends on grain size and crusts, and we do not have these data.
what_it_is_not.ilmenite: This is not a detection. Ilmenite also occurs in gabbro and other rocks. Most basalt holds only a few per cent of it. The class 'possible' means only that the rock type can hold iron-titanium oxide.

fields.<estimate>.figures: the figures that produced the word, null where unknown

mars_estimates.null_rule: unknown is null, never 0; a rule whose inputs are unknown gives null unless a known input settles it on its own (for example under a quarter bare gives low rockiness whatever the slope)
mars_estimates.coarse_warning: Every input here is a grid or map value (NASA POWER grids of 55 km and 1 degree, a rock map of 0.5 degree boxes, a 1 km permafrost model, 90 m heights). None of these estimates is a measurement at the place.

part_notes: Rock class: the GLiM half-degree box that is the square itself.
Anorthosite body: a listed body whose radius plus half the square's diagonal reaches the square's centre (our own test here; cells_scored.json covers only the Moon part).

Rockiness: slopes from mars_terrain.json are taken across about 3.7 km on ETOPO 2022 heights, so they read far flatter than 90 m slopes, and no roughness is held: the Mars part has fewer 'high' than the Moon part for that reason, not because the ground is smoother.
Permafrost: the map covers land from 25 N northward; Antarctic squares use the literature note; elsewhere without a map value, ground ice is unlikely by the yearly-mean-air test of rule 4 or null.

planet_factors.what: Figures that exist only on the Moon or Mars, for the 16 lunar regions (moon_cards.json) and the 57 Mars sites (mars_sites.json). Nothing already on those cards is repeated; links point to it.

meta.what: Figures that exist only on the Moon or Mars, for the 16 lunar regions (moon_cards.json) and the 57 Mars sites (mars_sites.json). Nothing already on those cards is repeated; links point to it.
meta.how_to_rerun: uv run python scripts/build_planet_factors.py   (add --offline to use saved files only)

kinds.measured: read from an orbital map at the site's coordinates; a map pixel or bin, never a measurement on the ground at the landing point (see scope)
kinds.model: a model value (e.g. the Mars Climate Database)
kinds.published figure: a number or sentence copied from a saved NASA page or paper
kinds.null: no figure; the note says why

meta.value_text: Where a published source gives words or a range instead of one number, value is null or a [low, high] pair and value_text holds the words to show.
meta.raw_folder: data/raw/planet_factors (every download logged in a _downloads.tsv beside it)

factors.name: Thermal inertia
factors.what_it_is: How strongly the top few centimetres of ground resist heating and cooling. Loose dust is low (below about 100), sand and crusted soil middle, rock and ice-cemented ground high.

factors.name: Rock abundance
factors.what_it_is: Share of the ground covered by rocks big enough to stay warm at night (Diviner: about 1 m and larger; Viking IRTM: about 15 cm and larger), from night-time thermal infrared.

connecting-ridge.source: LRO Diviner Level 3 rock abundance, label dgdr_ra_avg_cyl_128_img.lbl
connecting-ridge.note: Confirmed: the Diviner rock-abundance map covers latitudes -80 to 80 deg only (label MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE). This region's centre is at -89.46 deg, poleward of the map's edge, so Diviner publishes no rock abundance here. No other public lunar polar rock-abundance map was found.

factors.name: Near-surface hydrogen or water
factors.what_it_is: Hydrogen in the top tens of centimetres to about a metre, seen from orbit by the neutrons or gamma rays the ground gives off. Moon: hydrogen in ppm by weight. Mars: the same signal expressed as water (H2O) in weight per cent.
factors.unit: Moon: ppm H by weight; Mars: weight % H2O

connecting-ridge.source: Lunar Prospector neutron spectrometer, 'Hydrogen_halfdeg' (Feldman et al. 2001), PDS Geosciences Node
connecting-ridge.note: Half-degree bin holding the region centre; 264 bins centred inside the region range 143.8 to 147.4 ppm. The instrument's footprint is tens of kilometres, much wider than a half-degree bin near the pole, so this is a regional value, not a measurement at the landing point. It cannot tell ice in a cold trap from hydrogen spread through the soil.
connecting-ridge.scope: regional (orbital neutron footprint of tens of km)

phoenix.source: Arvidson et al. 2009, JGR 114, E00E02 (Phoenix Robotic Arm), abstract
phoenix.note: The lander measured this depth in trenches that it dug at the site. The abstract of the paper tells of '3-5 cm deep icy soil interfaces' in the trenches. NASA's photojournal for the Dodo-Goldilocks trench (dug 12 June 2008, 7 to 8 cm deep) shows white material in its upper part. Later, this material was found to be ice.
phoenix.value_text: 3 to 5 cm (dug by the lander's arm)

arcadia-planitia.source: SWIM project: Morgan et al. 2021, Nature Astronomy (manuscript on NASA NTRS 20205008958)
arcadia-planitia.note: No publication gives a single depth. The SWIM paper concludes that ice is 'present close to the surface in Arcadia'. It maps a radar reflector at depths of 15 to more than 100 m and reads it as the base of an ice-bearing layer. SWIM's own map files (swim.psi.edu) did not answer when we asked for them (HTTP 523). Thus we read no value at the coordinates of the site.
arcadia-planitia.value_text: close to the surface (published words); an ice-bearing layer to a depth of 15 to >100 m

deuteronilus-mensae.source: SWIM project: Morgan et al. 2021, Nature Astronomy (manuscript on NASA NTRS 20205008958)
deuteronilus-mensae.note: No publication gives a single depth. For the glaciers of Deuteronilus Mensae, the paper gives two readings. The ice is under a very thin debris cover of less than 2 m, or under meters of highly porous material. SWIM's map files did not answer when we asked for them (HTTP 523).
deuteronilus-mensae.value_text: under less than 2 m of debris, or under metres of porous material (two published readings)

jezero.note: We found no public figure. Jezero (18.4 N) is inside the SWIM study area. But we were not able to get SWIM's map files. Fig. 1a of the paper puts the theoretical 3 m zone of ice stability far from the site, in the direction of the pole.

gale.note: We found no public figure. Gale (4.6 S) is south of the SWIM study area (equator to 60 N). We found no map of ice depth for it.

factors.name: Quakes
factors.what_it_is: Ground shaking from inside the planet. Moon: shallow moonquakes from faults as the Moon cools and shrinks. Mars: marsquakes heard by NASA's InSight lander (2018-2022).

connecting-ridge.source: NASA release, 25 January 2024 (Watters et al. 2024, Planetary Science Journal)
connecting-ridge.note: The strongest shallow moonquake recorded by the Apollo seismometers (1969-1977) had its epicentre in the south-polar region, but its exact place could not be fixed; the cloud of possible epicentres covers many Artemis III candidate regions. Young thrust-fault scarps lie near and inside some of them. No count or rate is published for this region; no seismometer has worked near the south pole.
connecting-ridge.value_text: strong shallow moonquakes possible in the south-polar region; no local count
